strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored limitation of video-to-audio generation: models may be semantically synchronized yet fail to modulate sound according to physical event strength. Framing mass and velocity as explicit conditioning signals is a meaningful contribution for physically grounded audiovisual generation.

The proposed system is technically coherent: a Physics Parameter Estimator extracts moving objects, mass, and 3D velocity, while the Phy-Adapter injects mass and velocity through residual AdaLN modulation. The design is plausible and integrates well with a strong latent diffusion V2A backbone.

The empirical results are promising. PAVAS improves over MMAudio-L on APCC-delta, FD-PaSST, FD-PANNs, KL metrics, IS, and ImageBind score, while maintaining similar DeSync. User-study scores also favor PAVAS on audio quality, semantic alignment, temporal alignment, and physical plausibility.

The ablation study supports the main architectural claim: mass-only and velocity-only conditioning both improve metrics over the backbone, their combination is best, and delta-modulation outperforms direct summation.

Introducing VGG-Impact and APCC is useful. Even if imperfect, a benchmark and metric aimed specifically at physical plausibility can stimulate better evaluation beyond generic distributional or synchronization scores.
weaknesses: The central physical-grounding claim is under-supported in the main manuscript because the accuracy of the mass and velocity estimators is deferred to supplementary material. Since these estimates are the foundation of both conditioning and evaluation, their reliability should be visible and quantitatively justified in the paper itself.

APCC has a potential circularity/confounding issue: the same predicted physical quantities used to condition the generator are also used to evaluate physical consistency. Without ground-truth or independently validated mass/velocity on VGG-Impact, a lower APCC-delta may partly reflect alignment to estimator biases rather than true physical realism.

The APCC metric is only loosely justified physically. Acoustic onset strength is affected by material, contact geometry, room acoustics, microphone gain, occlusion, and source distance, while the metric mainly correlates it with estimated kinetic-energy change. This simplification is reasonable as a first proxy, but too weak to fully substantiate claims of physical correctness.

The comparison protocol has fairness caveats. PAVAS-L and MMAudio-L operate at 44.1 kHz while most other baselines are 16 kHz, some baselines do not use text input at test time, and several results come from author-provided samples rather than uniform reruns. These differences make the broad ranking less clean.

VGG-Impact is small, with 272 impact moments over 10 classes, and the paper does not report confidence intervals or statistical significance for APCC differences. This makes it hard to judge robustness of the physical-evaluation conclusions.

The method depends on many large pretrained modules, including VLM-based moving-object discovery and mass estimation, segmentation, and dynamic 3D reconstruction. This raises computational and reproducibility concerns, especially because prompts and implementation details are largely deferred to supplementary material.
The user study has only 15 participants and reports Likert means without statistical tests. It supports the trend but is not strong evidence for the perceptual or physical-plausibility claims.

The paper sometimes overstates the scope of 'physics-aware' generation. It models mass and velocity, but many sound-determining factors such as material stiffness, elasticity, contact type, surface geometry, and environment acoustics are not explicitly handled.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored limitation of current video-to-audio generation: sounds may be semantically synchronized while failing to vary plausibly with object dynamics. Conditioning generation on explicit physical quantities is a useful direction for computer vision and audio-visual modeling.

The proposed system is reasonably well motivated and integrates mass and velocity cues into a strong latent diffusion V2A backbone via a lightweight adapter. The design of residual AdaLN/FiLM-style physics modulation is plausible and locally ablated against direct summation.

The manuscript compares against a broad set of recent V2A baselines and includes both automatic metrics and a human study. The strongest baseline, MMAudio-L, is included, and PAVAS shows improvements on several metrics, including FDPaSST, FDPANNs, KL, ImageBind score, user-rated physical plausibility, and the proposed APCC-Delta.

The VGG-Impact subset and the attempt to define a physics-oriented metric are potentially useful contributions, since existing V2A evaluations mostly emphasize distributional fidelity, semantic alignment, and synchronization rather than physically meaningful variation.
weaknesses: The central physical grounding claim is not adequately supported in the main paper. Mass is inferred by a VLM from visual/semantic context and velocity is estimated from segmentation plus monocular dynamic 3D reconstruction, but the main paper provides no quantitative validation of these estimates beyond saying details are in supplementary material. Since the generated audio is conditioned on these estimates and APCC also depends on predicted physical quantities, the reliability of the entire physics claim rests on unshown evidence.

The proposed APCC evaluation is vulnerable to circularity and may measure consistency with the authors' estimator rather than real physics. Kinetic energy change is computed from predicted mass and pre/post velocities, not ground-truth physical measurements. If the same noisy or category-biased estimates are used to condition PAVAS and evaluate it, the metric can favor the proposed method without demonstrating actual physical realism.

The physical model is oversimplified. Impact sound energy and timbre depend strongly on material, geometry, contact area, damping, surface compliance, and microphone/acoustic environment, yet the method focuses on mass and centroid velocity. The paper claims physical plausibility from correlation between estimated kinetic energy change and onset spectral strength, but does not show that this correlation is stable or sufficient across the diverse VGGSound events considered.

The VGG-Impact benchmark is small and underspecified: 10 classes and 272 impact moments, manually filtered, with no clear annotation protocol, inter-annotator agreement, train/test contamination discussion, or release/reproducibility details in the main manuscript. This is a weak basis for a new metric and for broad claims about physical grounding.

The comparison protocol is not fully fair or clearly controlled. PAVAS-L and MMAudio-L operate at 44.1 kHz while most other baselines run at 16 kHz; some results are reproduced from code while others are evaluated from author-provided samples; some models use text at test time while others do not. These differences make the broad ranking less conclusive.

The gains over the strongest baseline are mixed and sometimes modest. Compared with MMAudio-L, PAVAS-L improves several distributional and subjective scores, but DeSync is slightly worse and FDVGG is worse. The user study improvements are reported with large standard deviations and no statistical significance test, so it is unclear whether the subjective gains are robust.

The ablation study does not directly validate the main physics contribution. Table 3 reports FDPaSST, IS, ImageBind, and DeSync, but not APCC-Delta or human physical plausibility for the mass-only, velocity-only, and adapter variants. This leaves unclear whether the physics inputs specifically improve physical consistency rather than general audio quality metrics.

Important baselines and controls are missing. The paper does not report random/noisy physics controls, category-average mass controls, oracle/manual physics controls, visual-feature-only object-mask controls, or conditioning on class/action labels alone. These are necessary to establish that the model benefits from instance-level physical estimates rather than dataset/category priors.

Reproducibility is limited. The pipeline depends on many large pretrained components, VLM prompts, manual filtering, object discovery, segmentation, CUT3R reconstruction, normalization statistics, and adapter details, many of which are deferred to supplementary material. The abstract also contains a placeholder-style 'Visit for demo videos,' which suggests incomplete presentation.

The method's originality is moderate rather than strong. The paper largely combines existing components: a VLM for mass/object descriptions, Florence/SAM2 for masks, CUT3R for 3D reconstruction, MMAudio-like diffusion training, and FiLM/AdaLN conditioning. The conceptual framing is interesting, but the technical novelty is not yet backed by sufficiently rigorous evidence.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and underexplored limitation of current video-to-audio systems: they can be semantically synchronized while failing to modulate sound according to physical factors such as mass and velocity. This is a meaningful problem for realistic audiovisual generation.

The proposed PAVAS pipeline is technically plausible and well motivated: object-level mass and velocity are estimated from video, transformed by a physics-aware adapter, and injected into a strong latent diffusion V2A backbone through residual modulation. The adapter design is sensible and the ablations support that mass and velocity conditioning improve over simply training the backbone longer.

The empirical results are strong overall. PAVAS improves over MMAudio-L on most reported VGGSound metrics, including FD_PaSST, FD_PANNs, KL, ImageBind score, and APCC-Delta, while maintaining similar temporal alignment. The human study also favors PAVAS across audio quality, semantic alignment, temporal alignment, and physical plausibility.

The VGG-Impact subset and APCC metric are useful contributions because they encourage evaluation of physical consistency rather than only perceptual quality or semantic alignment. Even if imperfect, this is a constructive step for the field.

The manuscript is generally clear, with a coherent pipeline figure, explicit equations for velocity estimation and conditioning, and enough implementation detail to understand the main training setup.
weaknesses: The central physical-realism evaluation is not fully convincing. APCC uses estimated mass and velocity rather than ground-truth physical measurements, and these same estimated cues are also used as conditioning inputs to PAVAS. This creates a risk that the metric rewards consistency with the model's own proxy estimates rather than true physical correctness.

VGG-Impact is quite small, with 272 impact moments across 10 classes. This is useful as a targeted diagnostic, but it limits the strength of broad claims about physical realism across open-world V2A generation.

The reliability of the Physics Parameter Estimator is crucial, but the main paper largely defers mass and velocity validation to the supplementary material. Since PPE errors directly affect both conditioning and APCC, stronger in-paper evidence is needed to support claims that the estimated physical quantities are accurate enough for the proposed conclusions.

Some comparisons are not perfectly controlled. PAVAS-L and MMAudio-L run at 44.1 kHz while several baselines run at 16 kHz; some results are reproduced, some are from author-provided samples, and some models differ in whether they use text input. These differences do not invalidate the results but weaken the interpretation of the leaderboard-style comparison.

The method depends on a large stack of pretrained components, including a VLM, Florence-2/SAM2-style segmentation, CUT3R reconstruction, CLIP/Synchformer encoders, and the diffusion backbone. The paper does not sufficiently discuss computational cost, failure modes, or how robust the pipeline is when object detection, segmentation, or 3D reconstruction fails.

The ablation table focuses on general audio metrics and does not clearly show the effect of each component on the proposed physical-consistency metric. For a physics-aware paper, APCC ablations for mass-only, velocity-only, direct summation, and Delta-modulation would be especially important.

The human study is encouraging but small, with 15 participants and limited protocol detail in the main paper. Statistical significance or preference-test details would make the subjective evidence stronger.

strengths: The paper tackles a meaningful limitation of current video-to-audio generation: models can be temporally and semantically plausible while ignoring physically relevant variation such as impact strength, mass, and velocity. This is a well-motivated contribution for audiovisual generation.

The proposed system is technically coherent: a strong latent diffusion/MMAudio-style backbone is augmented with explicit object-level mass and velocity estimates, object-centric features, and a gated residual AdaLN modulation mechanism. The design is plausible and the ablations support the utility of both mass and velocity cues as well as the delta-modulation strategy.

The experimental package is fairly broad. The paper compares against many recent V2A systems, reports standard distributional, semantic, temporal, and subjective metrics, includes a user study, evaluates model scales, and provides robustness/fallback analyses for noisy or missing physics cues.

The VGG-Impact benchmark and APCC metric are useful attempts to formalize physical consistency in V2A, an aspect not well captured by common audio fidelity or synchronization metrics. The APCC robustness checks with shuffled/noisy physical quantities are a good sign that the metric is not entirely arbitrary.

Results are generally favorable. PAVAS-L improves over MMAudio-L on APCC-delta, FD_PaSST, FD_PANNs, KL metrics, ImageBind score, and human ratings, while maintaining similar temporal synchronization. The gains in subjective physical plausibility are especially aligned with the paper's main claim.

The supplementary material gives substantial implementation detail, including VLM prompts, PPE module choices, training settings, runtime, missing-observation handling, and user study setup, which improves clarity and partial reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central physical-realism evidence is partly circular. PAVAS is conditioned on estimated mass/velocity from PPE, and APCC also uses estimated physical quantities rather than independently measured physical ground truth on VGG-Impact. This makes it difficult to separate true physical grounding from matching the biases/noise of the estimator used by both the model and the metric.

VGG-Impact is small and manually filtered: only 10 classes and 272 impact moments, with clips removed when contact dynamics or masks are unreliable. This is reasonable for a first benchmark but limits claims about broad physical realism in unconstrained videos and may favor cases where the proposed PPE pipeline works well.

The PPE validation is not fully convincing for the target setting. Mass estimation is evaluated on ABO objects rather than dynamic videos, and velocity estimation uses STARSS23 displacement as a proxy with manually filtered segmentations. These tests support plausibility but do not establish reliable per-object mass/velocity estimation in the VGGSound/VGG-Impact conditions where the model is evaluated.

Some comparisons are not perfectly controlled. PAVAS-L and MMAudio-L operate at 44.1 kHz, while several baselines are 16 kHz; some baselines are evaluated from author-provided samples and others from reproduced code; all models may not have the same text-conditioning setup. These differences complicate attribution of gains to physics awareness alone.

The improvement over the strongest baseline is mixed on some metrics. PAVAS-L has essentially unchanged DeSync relative to MMAudio-L, slightly worse FD_VGG on VGGSound, and in the non-impact/impact split has worse FD_VGG, IS, and DeSync in some cases. The paper's broad statement that it improves audio quality should be tempered accordingly.

The user study is helpful but small in video diversity: 27 participants rate only eight VGGSound clips. This is enough for supporting evidence, but not strong enough to conclusively validate perceptual physical plausibility across the diverse scenarios claimed.

The method is computationally heavy and operationally complex, requiring a VLM, Florence-2/SAM2, CUT3R, CLIP/Synchformer encoders, and a large diffusion model. Runtime is reported, but the dependency stack and reliance on proprietary-scale pretrained components may make reproduction and deployment difficult.

The physical model is simplified: kinetic-energy drop and onset spectral energy are reasonable for impacts, but many real sounds depend strongly on material, geometry, boundary conditions, contact duration, resonance, and environment. The method discusses material mostly through appearance/text cues rather than explicit physical modeling, so the term 'physics-aware' should be interpreted narrowly.

strengths: The paper addresses an interesting and underexplored limitation of video-to-audio generation: generated sounds may be semantically synchronized yet insensitive to physical quantities such as mass and velocity. This is a meaningful direction for CV/audio-visual generation.

The proposed pipeline is reasonably well specified at the systems level. The manuscript describes the PPE stack, mass and velocity conditioning, FiLM-style modulation, gated residual Delta-modulation into AdaLN, training stages, model sizes, prompts, and runtime costs.

The empirical section is broader than a minimal submission: it compares against several recent V2A systems, includes automatic metrics, a small user study, qualitative spectrogram comparisons, ablations for mass/velocity and injection strategy, robustness tests, and supplemental estimator evaluations.

The headline results show some supported gains over the strongest baseline MMAudio-L: lower APCC-delta, better FD_PaSST/FD_PANNs/KL/ImageBind, and higher user-study scores, while the ablation suggests both mass and velocity conditioning contribute beyond simply training longer.
weaknesses: The central claim of physical grounding is not convincingly established. The physical variables are estimated by the authors' own PPE, and APCC also uses these estimated physical quantities to evaluate generated audio. This creates a risk that the method is optimized and judged against the same noisy proxy rather than against independently measured physical ground truth.

The proposed APCC metric is only weakly validated. It correlates estimated kinetic-energy drops with onset strength, but real impact acoustics depend strongly on material, contact geometry, resonance, microphone distance, scene acoustics, and occlusion. The paper does not show that APCC aligns with human judgments of physical realism beyond the small user study, nor does it rule out trivial loudness/onset correlations.

VGG-Impact is small and potentially biased: 272 impact moments from 10 VGGSound classes, manually filtered to retain clear interactions and reliable object/mask tracks. Since difficult cases with ambiguous contacts or failed masks are removed, the benchmark may overstate the practicality of the PPE-based approach.

The physics estimator evidence is not strong enough for the claims. Mass estimation is evaluated on ABO object images, not in-the-wild videos with occlusion and scale ambiguity. Velocity estimation is evaluated on a proxy STARSS23 setup with 256 clips and tolerance ranges rather than direct metric velocity ground truth. Yet the main paper says the estimators are reliable and comparable to or better than expert models.

Many improvements are modest or mixed. Against MMAudio-L, PAVAS-L improves APCC-delta from 0.536 to 0.378 and several FD/KL metrics, but worsens FD_VGG (0.97 to 1.15) and slightly worsens DeSync (0.442 to 0.446). The ablation on the small backbone improves FD_PaSST and IS but barely changes ImageBind, and velocity-only appears to drive the DeSync gain. This is a weaker empirical case than the narrative suggests.

The baseline comparison has confounds. Methods differ in text conditioning, sample rate, parameter count, training data, and whether results are reproduced or taken from author-provided samples. PAVAS also uses the VGGSound class label as text input, while several baselines are marked as not using text input at test time, making some comparisons less clean.

The user study is too small to carry much evidential weight: only eight clips and 27 participants, with no statistical significance tests, confidence intervals for pairwise differences, or analysis of whether participants can reliably judge the stated physical plausibility dimension.

Originality is moderate rather than strong. The contribution is largely a composition of existing VLM, open-vocabulary segmentation, dynamic 3D reconstruction, and a diffusion V2A backbone with an adapter. The adapter design is plausible, but the conceptual novelty is incremental unless the physical-grounding evidence is much stronger.

Reproducibility remains limited. The method depends on many large pretrained systems, substantial H100 training, manual benchmark filtering, generated prompts, and author-curated impact annotations. The paper provides useful implementation details, but without code, annotations, and curation rules, reproducing the benchmark and APCC numbers would be difficult.

Overall, the paper has a worthwhile idea and some promising results, but the core scientific claim rests on noisy self-estimated physics and a newly proposed metric whose validity is not yet sufficiently demonstrated. The balance therefore favors weak rejection rather than acceptance.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely limitation of video-to-audio generation: current models can be semantically and temporally aligned while still producing sounds that ignore visible physical causes such as mass, impact strength, and velocity. The motivation is clear and the proposed physics-aware framing is a meaningful contribution.

PAVAS is technically well developed. The pipeline combines moving-object discovery, VLM-based mass estimation, segmentation plus dynamic 3D reconstruction for velocity estimation, and a gated residual Phy-Adapter for injecting mass and velocity into a diffusion transformer. The design is plausible and reasonably well specified.

The evaluation is broader than typical V2A papers. The authors compare against many recent baselines, report standard distributional, quality, semantic, and synchronization metrics, add a user study, and provide ablations for mass-only, velocity-only, direct summation, longer training, model scale, fallback behavior, and perturbation robustness.

The proposed VGG-Impact subset and APCC metric are useful steps toward evaluating physical plausibility, an aspect that existing V2A benchmarks largely miss. Even if imperfect, this benchmark encourages a more diagnostic evaluation protocol for physics-sensitive audio events.

Results are consistently favorable. PAVAS-L improves APCC-Delta substantially over MMAudio-L on VGGSound/VGG-Impact style evaluation, improves most objective audio metrics, and receives higher subjective ratings, especially for physical plausibility. The ablations support the claim that explicit physical cues help beyond simply training the backbone longer.

The supplementary material improves clarity and reproducibility by giving model variants, prompts, optimizer details, runtime profiling, invalid-estimate statistics, APCC definitions, and additional qualitative examples.
weaknesses: The central physical-realism evidence depends heavily on estimated physical quantities rather than independent ground-truth mass/velocity annotations. APCC uses PPE-derived kinetic energy estimates, and PAVAS is conditioned on related PPE outputs, so the metric may partly reward consistency with the system's own estimator rather than true physical correctness.

VGG-Impact is small, manually filtered, and limited to 10 impact classes with 272 moments. This is useful as a focused benchmark, but it leaves uncertainty about generalization to broader object interactions, deformable objects, continuous sounds, multi-source scenes, and cases where material or contact geometry dominates over mass/velocity.

The mass estimator is a VLM prompt-based module, which is creative but scientifically fragile. ABO evaluation suggests plausible estimates, but mass in unconstrained videos can be ambiguous, and the method may encode category priors more than visual evidence. The paper would be stronger with more independent validation of PPE on video data and with analysis of failure cases where VLM priors are misleading.

Baseline comparisons have some fairness caveats. PAVAS-L and MMAudio-L run at 44.1 kHz while several baselines run at 16 kHz; some results are reproduced while others use author-provided samples; and PAVAS benefits from multiple large pretrained components whose inference cost and failure modes are not reflected in parameter counts.

The user study is positive but narrow: 27 participants rate only eight clips. This supports perceptual quality but is not enough by itself to establish robust human preference across the diverse event classes claimed by the paper.

The ablation evidence shows improvements from mass and velocity conditioning, but the gains in some standard metrics are modest and not always uniform, e.g. FDVGG worsens versus MMAudio-L in the main table. The paper could more clearly separate improvements in general audio fidelity from improvements specifically attributable to physical grounding.

Reproducibility remains challenging despite good implementation details. Training requires large-scale data, H100 GPUs, precomputed embeddings, Qwen2.5-VL, Florence-2/SAM2, CUT3R, vocoders, and manual benchmark filtering. Without released code, generated samples, and VGG-Impact annotations, independent reproduction would be difficult.
